passages.title: The Rise of the Urban Beehive
passages.intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past two decades, beehives have appeared in some unlikely places: on the roofs of hotels in Paris, on the balconies of apartment blocks in Tokyo and among the vegetable beds of community gardens in Melbourne. In London alone, the number of registered hives more than doubled between 2008 and 2018, and some estimates now put the city's honeybee population at well over five thousand colonies. What began as the hobby of a few enthusiasts has become a visible symbol of the movement to bring nature back into cities.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The appeal is easy to understand. Honeybees are widely associated with environmental health, and news reports about declining bee populations, which became common in the mid-2000s, encouraged many people to see beekeeping as a practical way to help. Businesses were quick to notice the public's enthusiasm. A rooftop hive is cheap to install compared with other green initiatives, and companies have used them to demonstrate their environmental credentials, often selling or giving away the honey with their brand on the jar.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Urban bees appear to do surprisingly well. Cities offer a long flowering season: parks, gardens, street trees and window boxes provide a variety of plants from early spring until late autumn, and temperatures in built-up areas are usually a few degrees higher than in the surrounding countryside. Moreover, urban honeybees are often exposed to fewer agricultural pesticides than rural colonies. Several studies have found that hives in cities produce as much honey as, or more than, those on farmland, where large fields of a single crop may provide plenty of food for a few weeks but very little for the rest of the year.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: However, ecologists have begun to question whether the boom in urban beekeeping is actually good for nature. The honeybee is just one of around 20,000 bee species worldwide, and in most countries it is effectively a managed farm animal rather than a wild insect. Britain, for example, has around 270 species of bee, most of which live alone rather than in colonies and nest in the ground or in hollow plant stems. These wild bees are frequently more efficient pollinators of certain plants than honeybees, and many of them are in genuine decline because of habitat loss.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The concern is competition. A single strong honeybee colony may contain 50,000 workers at the height of summer, and together they can collect the pollen and nectar from a very large number of flowers each day. A study of one large city compared the number of hives in different districts with the amount of flower resources available, and concluded that in central areas the demand from honeybees was already greater than the supply that local plants could provide. When food runs short, the researchers argued, it is the wild species, with their smaller foraging ranges, that are most likely to suffer.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also concerns about disease. Managed honeybees can carry viruses and parasites that may be transmitted to wild bees when they visit the same flowers. Although the evidence for this is still limited, some scientists recommend that new hives should not be placed close to nature reserves or other sites known to be important for rare species.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that city beekeeping should be banned, and many beekeepers are responding to the criticism. Some associations now encourage members to plant pollinator-friendly flowers before adding new hives, and a number of cities have produced guidance on how many colonies an area can support. Conservation groups argue that individuals and companies who want to help bees would often achieve more by creating habitat — leaving areas of grass uncut, planting native wildflowers or building nesting sites for solitary bees — than by installing a hive. As one researcher put it, ‘Keeping honeybees to save bees is a little like keeping chickens to save birds.’

passages.title: Why Teenagers Sleep Late
passages.intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Parents have long complained that teenagers stay up too late and are impossible to wake in the morning. For much of the twentieth century this behaviour was regarded as a matter of discipline: young people, it was assumed, simply lacked the self-control to go to bed at a sensible hour. Research over the last thirty years has challenged this view, suggesting that the shift towards later sleep is, at least in part, biological.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The key lies in the body's internal clock, the circadian rhythm, which regulates when we feel alert and when we feel sleepy. One important signal is the hormone melatonin, which the brain releases in the evening as light fades. Laboratory studies have found that during puberty melatonin is released later in the evening than in younger children or adults, in some cases by up to two hours. As a result, a typical sixteen-year-old may not feel tired until around eleven o'clock at night, however early they go to bed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second factor is what scientists call ‘sleep pressure’: the gradual build-up of the need for sleep during the hours we are awake. Studies led by Professor Tomás Ruiz suggested that in adolescents this pressure builds more slowly than in children. Teenagers can therefore stay awake longer in the evening without feeling exhausted, which reinforces the effect of the delayed body clock.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Modern life makes matters worse. Phones, tablets and computers emit blue light, which is particularly effective at suppressing melatonin. Dr Anika Sharma, who studies technology and health, points out that the problem is not only light but also engagement: messages, games and social media keep the brain active at precisely the time it should be winding down. In a survey of 3,000 secondary school students, she found that those who used screens in bed slept on average forty minutes less on school nights than those who did not.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The consequences are significant. Teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night, but many get less than seven during the school week, then try to make up the difference at weekends. Chronic sleep loss has been linked to poorer concentration and memory, low mood and a higher risk of accidents. Dr Helen Marsh, an educational psychologist, argues that because early school start times force adolescents to wake before their bodies are ready, many students are effectively being taught at the wrong time of day.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This argument has led some schools to experiment with later start times. In one district, moving the beginning of the school day from 7.50 to 8.45 a.m. resulted in students sleeping, on average, an extra 34 minutes per night. Attendance improved and the number of students falling asleep in class fell sharply. Not everyone is convinced, however. Professor Leo Brandt warns that later starts can cause practical problems for families and for after-school activities, and that the benefits may disappear if students simply go to bed later. Most researchers nevertheless agree that schools, parents and teenagers themselves all have a role to play: limiting screens before bed, keeping regular sleep times and, where possible, aligning the timetable with the biology of the adolescent brain.

passages.title: Can Happiness Be Measured?
passages.intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, governments judged the success of their countries largely by economic output. Gross domestic product (GDP), which measures the total value of goods and services produced, became the headline figure by which progress was assessed. Yet even the economists who developed it warned that it was never intended to measure well-being. A country's GDP rises when it spends money cleaning up after a disaster, and it says nothing about how income is shared or how people feel about their lives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Since the early 2000s, a growing number of governments and international organisations have tried to measure well-being directly. The most common approach is surprisingly simple: people are asked how satisfied they are with their lives, usually on a scale from 0 to 10. Some surveys go further, asking how happy or anxious people felt the previous day, or whether they feel that the things they do are worthwhile.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics argue that such answers are too subjective to be useful. A person's response may depend on the weather, on their mood that morning or on the order in which questions are asked. Cultural differences present a further difficulty: in some societies it is considered modest to avoid extreme answers, while in others people may feel pressure to appear content. Comparing average scores between countries, the critics say, may tell us more about cultural norms than about real differences in well-being.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Supporters of well-being measurement accept these problems but believe they are often exaggerated. Large surveys, they point out, average out the effect of individual moods, and the results relate in predictable ways to other evidence: people who report low life satisfaction are more likely to visit the doctor, to change jobs or to experience periods of unemployment. In my view, the most convincing evidence is that the scores respond to real events. When a region's unemployment rate rises, average life satisfaction falls; when people move from a noisy, polluted area to a quieter one, their reported well-being tends to improve.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The more difficult question is what governments should do with the data. Some researchers argue that well-being should replace GDP as the main measure of national success. This seems to me too ambitious. Economic growth still matters, particularly for poorer countries, and a single happiness score could easily be manipulated or misunderstood. A better approach is to use well-being data alongside traditional economic indicators, especially when deciding between policies. If two programmes cost the same, the one that produces a larger improvement in people's lives — measured directly — has a strong claim to be preferred.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some governments have begun to work in this way, publishing ‘well-being budgets’ that rank spending proposals according to their expected effect on mental health, child poverty and other quality-of-life measures. Early evaluations suggest that the approach encourages government departments to cooperate on problems that cut across their responsibilities, although it is still too soon to tell whether it has made people any happier.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the greatest value of measuring well-being is that it changes the questions policy-makers ask. Instead of focusing only on how much a country produces, they are encouraged to consider what kind of lives its citizens are able to lead. That alone, I would argue, is a significant step forward.
